title: Sleep and Memory

keyTerms.definition: the ability to keep information and remember it later
the process that makes a new, weak memory stronger and longer-lasting
weak and easily broken or lost
a stage of sleep when most dreaming happens

predictionQuestion: Is it a good idea to stay up all night studying before an exam? What do you think the lecturer will say?

segments.text: Hello, everyone. In this session, we're going to look at the connection between sleep and memory. Many students believe that staying up late to study is a good idea before an exam. What I want to show you today is why that belief may be wrong. I'll do this in three steps. I'll begin by explaining what happens to memories after we learn something. Then I'll describe the role of sleep. And lastly, I'll give you some practical advice.

Let's begin with memory. When you learn something new, for example a new word or a formula, the memory is quite fragile at first. To become stable and long-lasting, the memory needs to be strengthened. This process is called consolidation. In other words, consolidation is the process that turns a weak, new memory into a stronger one.

So where does sleep come in? A large part of consolidation seems to happen while we sleep. During sleep, the brain is not simply switched off. Instead, it is very active. It appears to replay and reorganise information from the day. As a result, important information is strengthened, and less useful information may be allowed to fade.

Sleep is not all the same, though. During the night, we move through different stages of sleep in cycles. Deep sleep is thought to be especially important for facts and information, such as names, dates and definitions. Another stage, often called dream sleep or REM sleep, seems to be linked to skills, and to connecting ideas in new ways.

Let me put this another way. If you study all evening and then sleep for only four hours, you may cut short the very process that helps you keep what you studied. Lack of sleep also affects attention, so the next day it is harder to concentrate and to learn anything new.

What does this mean in practice? There are three simple pieces of advice. The first is to spread your study over several days, rather than doing it all in one night. This gives your brain several nights of consolidation. The second is to keep a regular sleep routine. And the third is to review difficult material in the evening and then sleep on it. For instance, you could look over your vocabulary list before bed and test yourself the next morning.

To summarise, then. New memories are fragile and need to be consolidated. Much of this consolidation happens during sleep, when the brain replays and reorganises information. Different stages of sleep seem to support different kinds of memory. So, if you want to remember what you study, sleep is not wasted time. It is part of learning.

keyIdeas.text: Staying up late to study before an exam may be a bad idea.
New memories are fragile. They need consolidation to become stable and long-lasting.
A large part of consolidation seems to happen during sleep.
During sleep the brain is active: it replays and reorganises information from the day.
Important information is strengthened; less useful information may fade.
Different stages of sleep seem to support different kinds of memory.
Deep sleep: facts (names, dates, definitions). REM sleep: skills and connecting ideas.
Lack of sleep also hurts attention, so it is harder to concentrate the next day.
Advice: spread study over several days, keep a regular sleep routine, review then sleep on it.
Example: look at your vocabulary list before bed and test yourself in the morning.
